en: The painted spear that breaks the enemy
Was laid beneath his thigh.
Making Aktulpar bound forward,
The eight khans in the court—
Semetey, still in a frenzy,
Then entered among them.
Before them their dancers
They had dancing to and fro;
Great dutars with bellies filling an armful
They had their singers play.
They had their dutars plucked;
Some sixty young men
They had all sing akush songs.
They plucked their dutars;
They all made merry;
They were immersed in entertainment;
They were asking for the boy as a hostage.
Changing the beat of their drums,
They were about to play;
The boy as a hostage
They were about to take.
They were reciting voluntary prayers,
They were saddling their fine horses.
When they saw the boy's appearance,
They stood in fear.
If you ask how the boy looked—
Mist streamed from his mouth;
His mighty teeth, broad as doors,
Broke into pieces like millet;
Flames hissed from his mouth;
His bright front teeth, broad as spades,
Crackled whenever he clenched them.
Toward the Kushbegi, khan of Kokand,
He now rode, pressing close.
Riding up and pressing close, Semetey
Now spoke a reasoned word:
'Your father's grave! Say, Kokand,
You will be slaughtered;
Turn back, Kokand, every last one of you!
Alty-Shaar, khan of Kokand,
Go to your lands now without delay.
You will die, every last one of you;
You will suffer a blow from me.
Your father's grave, Andijan!
Do not prance in your blue overshoes;
Do not make your fine horse toss its head.
You will lodge in a place of suffering;
You will be slaughtered now.
If you turn back to look, you will die by me;
You will see the face of Judgment!
That you should ask to take me,
That you should carry me off as a hostage,
That you should put poison in my food,
That you should cut off my head,
That to all the enemies who grappled with me
You should carry the glad tidings,
That from them much gold
You should take as your share of booty,
That my twelve-year-old life
You should bring to an end—
You great lump of a Sart, born for mischief,
Have I plundered your possessions?
Have I wreaked havoc upon you?
Have I stolen your piebald horse?
Have I scattered your goods of pure gold?
Have I driven off your dun horse?
You harbored enmity in your belly;
Have I scattered the goods in your saddlebag?
Have I settled along your hills?
You stand here, people of six khans;
Have I reaped your barley unripe?
Seven khans, may you sink into the earth!
I have led away no caravan of yours.
That I should go as a hostage and be slaughtered,
That you should put me to death—
You have no seven generations' vengeance against me!
Say, Kokand, rein in your horse,
Kokand!'
The locked white saddlebag—
He hastily opened its mouth.
The ammunition that never diminished,
Temir Khan's Akbaran—
He poured it in by the handful.
He now took Akbaran in his hand;
The Sarts lying before him
He now assailed with its booming shots.
Making their fine horses toss their heads,
Prancing in their blue overshoes,
The men of Andijan fled one way.
Saying, 'You were the one who said it!'
Angrily blaming one another,
The men of Kokand fled another way.
'Whether one speaks or not, you will not leave off;
You leave no unspoken thought alone.
He will slaughter us all,' they said,
'Only slaughtering us will ease his spirit,' they said.
'He will plunder our possessions,' they said,
'He will bring calamity upon us,' they said.
'The prince's son—
Whoever molests him will not survive,' they said.
'Whoever talks back will not prosper,' they said.
The men of Margilan fled another way.
When Semetey reached twelve,
He now plundered their possessions;
He now wrought such havoc;
He now bore down upon their heads;
He now scattered their four kinds of livestock.
Some sixty of their champions
Lay dead in Bukhara.
An unrelenting onslaught
Semetey then unleashed.
Eighty mules fell into his hands;
Their goods became his prize,
And Semetey took them.
That the Sarts were enemies,
The boy now saw.
To Kanykei, living in exile,
Eighty mule-loads of goods
He now gave as tribute.
Only yesterday Kanykei had arrived in mourning,
And Semetey had come as a fugitive;
Now he prospered by plundering their goods.
The wolf-maned hero had come to Bukhara and grown;
No one could trouble him;
No one remained to turn a horse-catching pole against the boy.
His twelve bodily parts were in harmony;
Your wolf-maned hero became a lion like his father.
He grew unruly and prospered;
Your wolf-maned hero had entered Bukhara and grown;
A man became a marvel;
Became a lion who could overturn the world.
Temir Khan in Bukhara
Had something to say;
Of the twelve-year-old little one,
He had cause to be afraid.
Blackened with soot from quenching charcoal,
Possessor of many forests,
There was his youngest brother:
He had misgivings about Sary Taz.
Sary Taz, marked with a sign,
He suspected would cause trouble.
He had words he would not twist;
He spoke the truth straight out;
In his forehead was one eye as big as a bowl.
He was a younger brother than Koloi.
Poor Temir Khan had lost his sense;
Over the khanship of Bukhara,
They had contended for seven years.
They threw the settled people into turmoil,
Mounted stallions from the tethering lines,
Snatched up poles from the ground,
Cried out, 'Mercy!'
And fought a terrible battle.
People were slaughtered, warriors died;
The people's losses were great,
And Sary Taz was left destitute.
His paths lay through ravines;
His three elder brothers were his foes;
The poor fellow himself was bald,
And all the people of Bukhara were hostile.
Tuuchunak beneath him,
His winged steed, had been well fed;
The people were in turmoil and followed along;
He had no supporter at his side;
His own kin had become his enemies;
He had few days left to see.
They took his horse and left him on foot,
Made him master of Kul-Tokoi in Kuleshen
And set him to quenching charcoal.
Otherwise poor Sary Taz would perish.
Each month, eighty camel-loads of charcoal
To Temir Khan of Bukhara
He used to pay as tribute.
Unable to endure the tribute,
Sary Taz, his strength exhausted,
Wasted away quenching charcoal.
If the tribute fell short by one camel-load,
Sixty champions from Bukhara
Would drive him on and beat and strike him;
Your bald man would burn in the fire.
To Temir Khan's city,
Kanykei had come in exile, they said;
He would hear it from the tales.
The orphan Semetey had arrived,
And Ismail had taken him in, they said;
He would hear it from the people.
Sary Taz was a great man,
Piecing tale together with tale,
Questioning those who came.
Counting the days with sheep droppings,
Sary Taz lived in humiliation.
His kin had become enemy dogs;
Sary Taz lived under oppression.
Unrelenting hardship
Sary Taz continued to endure.
If Semetey came, of his father
Sary Taz meant to tell him.
With Semetey, to the Kyrgyz,
Sary Taz meant to depart.
To bring Temir Khan down,
Somehow contriving to find a way,
Sary Taz meant to achieve it.
'He has reached twelve,' he said,
'God has granted my wish,' he said.
He offers a prayer to Baabedin;
Sary Taz, that unfortunate kinsman,
Vows a sheep to Koroshon.
'When will He grant my wish?' he says.
'When will my orphan come?' he says.
In his home, a hut of grass,
Sary Taz spends his nights.
From Allah Most High alone,
'When will my orphan come?'
Sary Taz keeps asking.
The exploits of Sary Taz
The Bukharan knew beforehand,
The mischief of that unruly bald man.
'If he hears words from the woodcutter Taz,
If he hears, "Your lineage is different,"
Will he plunder my possessions?
Will he wreak thorough havoc?
Will he break into my treasury?
Will my orphan join him to bring me down?
Preparing and digging my pit,
Will my orphan boil up misery for me?
If that orphan lives on,
He will show us quite a spectacle!'
(He had something to say;
Temir Khan lived in fear
And had misgivings about Sary Taz.)
'Will the boy go to the forest?
Will Sary Taz unfold the boy's earliest ancestry,
And will they join to bring me down?
That swine has an old vengeance;
Will they join to bring me down?'
About his charcoal-burning bald man
He had fearful suspicions,
Frightened by his own fears, Temir Khan
Had an answer to give the boy.
He had misgivings about Sary Taz:
'Do not fly a falcon in the forest,'
Temir Khan had words he spoke each day.
Putting his belt about his neck,
Temir Khan would not leave off,
Pleading with Semetey:
'My spring feeding a river in its valley,
Semetey, my little one gained through mortal hardship,
Do not heed mischievous words.
In Kul-Tokoi of Kuleshen,
Do not fly your falcon laughing.
No man can have his fill of its delights;
In the forest of Kuleshen,
No one has flown a falcon laughing.
Whoever encountered it did not survive;
No one went there to meet it;
Whoever encountered it did not remain alive.
